title: Reciting Without Reciting
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: Throughout his life Mr. Jiang Weinong took prajñā as his doctrinal basis and Amitābha as his practice, deeply grasping the essentials of Buddha-recitation. At his life's end he said: “Golden light shines everywhere; the Buddha has come to receive me,” and passed away peacefully amid the sound of the Buddha's name.

inline.s: Throughout his life Mr. Jiang Weinong took prajñā as his doctrinal basis and Amitābha as his practice, deeply grasping the essentials of Buddha-recitation. At his life's end he said himself: “Golden light shines everywhere; the Buddha has come to receive me.” And he passed away peacefully amid the sound of the Buddha's name.
The following is his teaching in
Lectures on the Diamond Sutra

[The method of Buddha-recitation is, above all, the most expedient of expedients for cutting off thoughts. Not allowing other thoughts but reciting the Buddha's name is also a way of shifting one's thought. And recitation is even more intimate than the practice of visualization. Reciting the Buddha's name is a pure thought; exchanging it for a pure thought is to treat one's habitual defiled and turbid thoughts. And to recite single-mindedly is again to use a single, unified thought to treat one's habitual scattered and disordered thoughts.]

The method of reciting the Buddha's name is, above all, the most expedient of expedients for cutting off thoughts. Not allowing other thoughts to arise but reciting the Buddha's name is a way of shifting one's thought, and thus reciting the name is even more intimate and easy than visualization-recitation. Reciting the name is a pure thought; one uses a single pure thought to counteract one's habitual defiled and turbid thoughts. And one must recite single-mindedly, which again uses a single, unified thought to counteract one's habitual scattered and disordered thoughts.
The key point: use the pure thought to counteract defiled thoughts; use single-mindedness to counteract a scattered mind.

Pure thoughts create pure karma, the cause of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; defiled thoughts create defiled karma, the cause of falling into the six paths of transmigration. In our arising thoughts, how can we not be careful?
To turn from other thoughts to reciting the Buddha's name is to turn defiled karma into pure karma

[Moreover, Buddha means awakening; if every thought is the Buddha, then every thought is awakening. To be awakened is to awaken to the fact that one's nature is originally without thought — hence it is said to be even more intimate. If one can simply be earnest and single-minded, one can achieve
recitation without recitation
One should know that the aim of reciting the Buddha's name must ultimately return to no-thought

, that is, to return to suchness; then, without speaking of cutting off, thoughts are cut off of themselves, and without hoping for realization, realization comes of itself — what an expedient this is!]

Moreover, Buddha means awakening; if every thought is the Buddha, then every thought is awakening. To be awakened is to awaken to the fact that one's nature is originally without thought — hence it is said to be even more intimate. If one can simply recite single-mindedly and earnestly, one can achieve recitation without recitation.
One should know that the aim of reciting the Buddha's name must ultimately return to no-thought,

that is, to return to suchness (one's original nature); then, without speaking of cutting off thoughts, thoughts are cut off of themselves, and without seeking realization, realization comes of itself (realization: to see one's original nature thoroughly. This is the state of entering the samādhi of Buddha-recitation). What an expedient this is!

[Recitation without recitation] Reciting the Buddha's name with no-thought (not a single thought arising) is recitation of the true mark, reciting the dharmakāya Buddha. [Recitation of the true mark] Reciting the Buddha's name by means of ultimate emptiness and the dharma of nothing whatsoever. In the Buddha Treasury Sutra, the Buddha said:

“Śāriputra, what is it to be called reciting the Buddha? Seeing nothing whatsoever is called reciting the Buddha. Śāriputra, the Buddhas are immeasurable, inconceivable, beyond weighing and measuring; for this reason, seeing nothing whatsoever is called reciting the Buddha. The true is without discrimination, and the Buddhas are without discrimination; therefore it is said that the thought without discrimination is reciting the Buddha. Furthermore, seeing the true mark of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What is called the true mark of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever. It is by this dharma of ultimate emptiness and nothing whatsoever that one recites the Buddha. Furthermore, in this dharma, even the smallest thought is unobtainable — this is called reciting the Buddha. Śāriputra, this
(this)

method of reciting the Buddha severs the way of language, transcends all thoughts, and is the thought that cannot be obtained — this is called reciting the Buddha. Śāriputra, all thoughts are of the mark of quiescent cessation. To accord with this dharma is called cultivating the recitation of the Buddha. One should not recite the Buddha by means of form. Why? Reciting form grasps its marks, and craving its flavor becomes consciousness. Without shape and without form, without object and without nature — this is called reciting the Buddha. Therefore one should know: without discrimination, without grasping and without rejecting, this is true recitation of the Buddha.”

“Reciting the Buddha means breaking through all coarse and subtle thought, wholesome and unwholesome alike; being without coarse thought and without subtle thought, silently without any notion — this is called reciting the Buddha. Why? One should not recollect the Buddhas by means of coarse and subtle thought; being without coarse thought and without subtle thought is called pure recitation of the Buddha. In this recitation there is not even the subtle mental karma of mind and thought,
(in this recitation there is not even the subtle mental karma of mind)
, how much less the karma of body and speech
(how much less the coarse and evident karma of body and speech)

“These dharmas are all empty, without any essential nature; one cannot grasp a single mark in thought — this so-called marklessness is called true recitation of the Buddha. That is to say: unarisen and unperishing, markless and unconditioned.”
“The anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi of all the Buddhas is entirely without notion and without thought.”

[Coarse and subtle thought] In the new translation this is rendered “vitarka and vicāra,” and in the old translation “coarse and subtle thought.” Coarse reflection is called “vitarka” (jue), and subtle reflection is called “vicāra” (guan); both can disturb the mind in concentration.
[Even if one's recitation practice has not yet achieved
recitation without recitation

, as long as one's practice and vows are genuine and earnest, relying on Amitābha's power of compassionate vows one will be received and reborn there, attaining the state of the avaivartika — here called non-retrogression, which is the position of the first abode. If one practiced other methods, one would need to pass through countless distant kalpas to reach this; now it is accomplished in a single lifetime, hence it is called the expedient of expedients.]

Even if one's recitation practice has not yet achieved recitation without recitation, as long as one's practice and vows are genuine and earnest, relying on Amitābha Buddha's power of compassionate vows one will be received and reborn there, attaining the state of the avaivartika. “Avaivartika,” in this land called “non-retrogression,” is the position of the bodhisattva of the first abode. If one practiced other Dharma gates, one would need to pass through countless distant kalpas before reaching this position. Now it is accomplished in a single lifetime, hence it is called the expedient of expedients.
[Avaivartika (ā
pí

bázhì)] A Sanskrit sound, translated into Chinese as “non-retrogression.” This means that after being born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one only advances step by step, all the way to Buddhahood, without ever falling back.

[However, for practice and vows to be genuine and earnest, one must be single-mindedly set on reciting the Buddha and seeking rebirth; only then can they be called genuine. If, while reciting on the one hand, one gives rise on the other to defiled and turbid thoughts, then one's practice and vows are not genuine.]

However, for practice and vows to be genuine and earnest, one must be single-mindedly set on reciting the Buddha and seeking rebirth; only then can they be called genuine. If, while reciting on the one hand, one gives rise on the other to defiled and turbid thoughts, then one's practice and vows are not genuine.
[If, while reciting on the one hand, one gives rise on the other to defiled and turbid thoughts]
Reciting on one side while entertaining deluded thoughts on the other. This is reciting with a scattered mind. Master Yinguang said:
“Reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind, one can hardly be reborn there. ... Reciting single-mindedly, one will certainly be reborn there.”
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,
Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou) He also said:
“If the six sense-faculties are not gathered in, then even while reciting the Buddha's name, deluded thoughts still fly about in confusion in the mind, and real benefit is hard to obtain.”
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,

Letter in Reply to Master Huanxiu) Therefore, a reciter of the Buddha's name should gather the mind in recitation, making the thoughts converge into one (all thoughts into one), and then even cut off thought entirely (the one returning to nothing).

[Therefore, even if a reciter of the Buddha's name cannot easily accomplish the level of cutting off thought, the two sentences “one should not let the mind arise dwelling on form, one should not let the mind arise dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas” must be carried out. Otherwise, one's vows are not earnest and one's practice not genuine — how could one be received by the Buddha? If the air of defilement and turbidity is heavy, and one is too much out of keeping with the two words “purity and stillness,” then even the Buddha can do nothing about it.]

Therefore, even if a reciter of the Buddha's name cannot easily accomplish the level of cutting off thought, the two sentences in the Diamond Sutra — “one should not let the mind arise dwelling on form, one should not let the mind arise dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas” — must be carried out. Otherwise, one's vows are not earnest and one's practice not genuine; how could one be received by the Buddha? If the air of defilement and turbidity is heavy, and one is too much out of keeping with the two words “purity and stillness,” then even Amitābha Buddha can do nothing about it.
[Mo ru zhi he] There is no help for it. [Ye yi yi] An exclamatory particle of very strong tone.

[One must know that the arising of thought is itself delusion; the thought of reciting the Buddha is also delusion, not the true. Why? Because the nature of suchness is originally without thought. But because the ordinary person's defiled thoughts do not cease, of necessity one borrows the pure thought of reciting the Buddha to treat the defiled thoughts that dwell on sense-objects. For (because) the thought of reciting the Buddha, though not the essence of suchness itself, is the wondrous function that tends toward suchness.]

One must know that the arising of thought is itself delusion; the thought of reciting the Buddha is also delusion, not the true. Why? Because the nature of suchness is originally without thought. But because the ordinary person's defiled thoughts do not cease, of necessity one borrows the pure thought of reciting the Buddha to counteract the defiled thoughts that dwell on the objects of the senses. For the thought of reciting the Buddha, though not the essence of suchness itself, is the wondrous function that tends toward suchness.

[Why? Suchness is the pure mind, and the Buddha-thought is a pure thought; both are pure, and so they correspond. Therefore the thought of reciting the Buddha, continuing thought after thought without cease, can reach no-thought — hence it is called the supreme expedient. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is also an illusory appearance, yet one cannot but seek and vow to be reborn there, because the pure illusion is not the same as the defiled illusion. Why? The pure land is originally manifested by the pure mind — as the saying goes, when the mind is pure, the land is pure.]

Why? Because suchness is the pure mind, and the thought of reciting the Buddha is a pure thought; both are pure, and therefore they correspond. Hence the thought of reciting the Buddha, continuing thought after thought without cease, can reach no-thought — which is why reciting the name is called the supreme expedient (the expedient of expedients). The Land of Ultimate Bliss is also an illusory appearance, yet one cannot but seek and vow to be reborn there, because the pure illusion is not the same as the defiled illusion. Why? The pure land is originally manifested by the pure mind — as the saying goes, when the mind is pure, the land is pure.

[One must know that when Amitābha comes to receive us, fundamentally he has never come; and when we are reborn in the West, fundamentally we have never gone. Though there is no going, what harm is there in manifesting coming and going? Why? Not-coming and not-going is the principle-essence; coming and going is the phenomenal appearance. Principle and phenomena have never been two; nature and mark must be perfectly fused. Therefore, although there is no coming and no going, this does not obstruct there being coming and going; although there is coming and going, in truth there is no coming and no going.]

One must know that when Amitābha Buddha comes to receive us, fundamentally he has never come; and when we are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, fundamentally we have never gone. Though there is no going, what harm is there in manifesting coming and going? Why? Not-coming and not-going is the principle-essence; coming and going is the phenomenal appearance. Principle and phenomena have never been two; nature and mark must be perfectly fused. Therefore, although there is no coming and no going, this does not obstruct there being coming and going; although there is coming and going, in truth there is no coming and no going.

[What is most important is that coming and going must be realized upon not-coming and not-going, and not-coming and not-going must be enacted through coming and going. This is the essential key to reciting the Buddha and seeking rebirth. With this key, one will certainly be reborn and see the Buddha. Who says that those who cultivate the Pure Land need not study prajñā, or suspects that prajñā obstructs the Pure Land?]

What is most important is that coming and going must be realized upon not-coming and not-going, and not-coming and not-going must be enacted through coming and going. This is the essential key to reciting the Buddha and seeking rebirth. One who gains this key will certainly be reborn and see the Buddha. Who says that those who cultivate the Pure Land need not study prajñā, and who would suspect that studying prajñā obstructs cultivating the Pure Land?

[Who says those who cultivate the Pure Land need not study prajñā, and suspects that prajñā obstructs the Pure Land?] The great Pure Land master, Layman Wang Longshu, wrote in Longshu's Expanded Writings on the Pure Land:
“The Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations
(the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life)

says: those of the highest grade of the highest rank of rebirth read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures and understand the supreme truth. Thus one who cultivates the highest grade must know the Buddha's profound purport.”

Layman Longshu himself was just so: he attained mastery over birth and death, knew in advance the time of his passing, and passed away standing up. [The supreme truth] The highest, most perfect, and ultimate truth. The true mark of all dharmas is the supreme truth. The Buddha said:

“All dharmas are false and unreal; following them to the point of their cessation is what is called the real, called the true mark, called the dharma realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the truth of the supreme meaning, called the emptiness of the supreme truth.”
The supreme truth is also called the truth of the supreme meaning. “Truth” (di) means the principle that is true and without error.
(The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
fascicle forty) [The true mark of all dharmas] The actual state of all dharmas. The Buddha Treasury Sutra says:
“What is called the true mark of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says:
“All dharmas are like illusory appearances; the Tathāgata dwells among them with the power of expedient means, without any defilement or attachment.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“The bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty and as their true mark, without inversion, without moving, without retreating, without turning.”
On the true mark of all dharmas, see
The True Mark of All Dharmas
[Jiang Weinong (

)] A famous great layman of the late Qing and early Republican period. He was originally from Jiangning, Jiangsu, and resided in Hubei. His lay name was Zhongye, and his Dharma name was Miaoxi. From childhood he recited the Diamond Sutra with his grandfather and often had spiritual responses. In the seventh year of the Republic (

), he took the Chan master Weijun as his teacher and received the bodhisattva precepts. That same year he also collated the ancient manuscripts among the Dunhuang collections. Over the course of two years, from the scattered and disordered volumes he compiled one fascicle of the Commentary on the Śālistambaka Sutra and two fascicles of the Collected Commentaries on the Vimalakīrti Sutra. In the tenth year of the Republic, he went east to Mount Kōya in Japan with the Japanese monk Juesui to study Shingon (Eastern Esoteric) Buddhism in depth. Later, for various reasons he could not remain in seclusion there and soon returned home. Afterwards, with Jian Zhaonan and others, he established the Gongdelin Buddhist Scripture Distribution Center in Shanghai, gathering printing blocks from the northern and southern scripture-printing centers and from various famous mountains to circulate throughout the country. In the fourteenth year of the Republic, he assisted the famous Tibetan esoteric master, the Venerable Bai Puren, in traveling about to propagate the esoteric teachings. The layman's wisdom and understanding surpassed the ordinary, his observance of the precepts was strict, and his realization of prajñā was deep. The Lectures on the Diamond Sutra that he wrote circulated very widely. At his life's end he said himself: “Golden light shines everywhere; the Buddha has come to receive me.” And he passed away peacefully amid the sound of the Buddha's name, at the age of sixty-six.
